prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, which established band topology protected by time-reversal symmetry in real materials

statement.case_for: My scientific case is unchanged and, after the full first round, firmer. Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2 invariant with protected edge states. Molenkamp's group then measured quantised edge conduction in HgTe wells, a test that could have failed. About eighteen years of reproduction in transport, ARPES and scanning probes, together with quantitative agreement with spin-orbit band-structure calculations, is the closure of theory, calculation and measured spectra that I weigh most. All eight members now either prefer B013 or list it first among their alternatives, and no file disputes the physics or the maturity. As to the question the chair asked about the 2016 prize, here is one sentence I can defend: the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and topological phases in model systems and quantum Hall-type states, while this recognition is for a symmetry-protected topological band insulator that was predicted from spin-orbit coupling in a specific material and then realised in a specific material.
statement.case_against: The attribution remains imperfect. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal told Molenkamp where to look and is outside the credited names, and Zhang's death removes one possible laureate. Hasan's ARPES work on 3D topological insulators is left out, so a citation that reaches for the topological insulators as a class would overclaim for these three people. The 2016 prize will lead some to ask about repetition. Device impact is still modest, as Kroll says. I accept these as costs of a three-seat limit, not as reasons to withhold a prize that is mature and uncontested on the science.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps Mele with Kane because the Z2 classification is a single theory contribution, and says that 3D topological insulators are a matter for the citation text, not for swapping a laureate.
responses.response: Agreed, and I should correct the record: several round-1 replies, including yours, describe me as proposing Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan. That was my opening ballot. In round 1 I already moved to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and I hold that now. Your argument about the Kane-Mele pair is the decisive one for me. On wording I would go slightly narrower than your citation: I would not say that the work established topological insulators as a new class of matter, because that phrase borrows credit from the 3D materials branch and from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. I would say that it established time-reversal-protected band topology in real materials, anchored to the 2D HgTe realisation.

responses.point: Kroll prefers Katori and Ye (B006) but names B013 as his first alternative. His reservation is that B013 has the harder allocation problem, and he is weighing whether to put the broadest support ahead of a cleaner attribution.
responses.response: Your point on attribution is fair: Katori and Ye are a cleaner pair than any trio for B013. But I would weigh the discovery content differently. Lattice clocks are a major advance in measurement that is still maturing, and you concede that the redefinition of the second is pending and that the discovery-versus-instrument question is open. B013 has a bounded and verifiable allocation problem, in which the missing credit is acknowledged in the citation and in the minutes, and a result that no member disputes scientifically. I would ask you whether you could accept B013 alone as a single-part final position. If not, I would rather see B006 as an alternative on the ballots than a second part, because adding it would turn a convergent prize into a split one.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that adding Hasan would open a second incomplete attribution, since the 3D branch also rests on Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents theory, and that a citation centred on the quantum spin Hall effect is cleaner.
responses.response: That argument persuades me and strengthens my move away from Hasan in the opening round. It also solves part of the BHZ problem: if we name the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and its HgTe realisation, the omission of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is a limit of the three-person rule that the citation does not misstate. I do not think a swap of Hasan for Molenkamp works either, because the HgTe experiment is the direct test of the Kane-Mele prediction. I would record in the committee minutes that the omission of Hasan and of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a matter of allocation under the rules, not a judgement on their importance.

responses.point: Johansson says that if the committee wants to honour the 3D route, it should be a separate discussion and not squeezed out of this trio, and he has moved from B009 to B013 after trying to be independent of his own field.
responses.response: I agree, and I value that you looked past your own field. On the 3D branch, I do not think a second part is justified in this configuration. A two-part prize would need three seats to be split and would put Kane, Mele and Molenkamp against Hasan and Fu, with the attribution for the 3D discovery still being unsettled and the 2016 overlap question doubled. I therefore treat the 3D ARPES discovery as something that may deserve consideration in a later year, and not as part of this prize.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asked whether the 3D branch is a separate achievement that deserves its own part, and noted that the trio can look like it skips a link in the chain.
responses.response: My answer is that the 3D branch is a distinct achievement and not a variant of the 2D one, but I do not think it belongs in this prize. It is distinct because it concerns surface states of a bulk insulator, observed by ARPES in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3, and its theory (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents) has a different cast. Within a three-person limit that cannot be added to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp without removing someone, and none of the three can be removed honestly. On your question about skipping a link: with the proposed wording we recognise the prediction and the first observation, which are the two ends of a chain whose middle link, the BHZ proposal, we acknowledge but cannot credit.

uncertainties: How the committee will word the difference from the 2016 prize. My sentence above is meant to be a defensible starting point, and I would accept any wording that is accurate about what the three people did.
Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and of Hasan, will be read outside the committee as an incomplete story. I judge this acceptable but not comfortable.
My knowledge of exact priority details, including the timing of the Kane-Mele and BHZ papers and the first HgTe measurements, is from memory and has not been checked against the primary papers.
Whether B025 (twisted bilayer graphene) or B021 (anyonic statistics) will mature enough in the next few years to be a stronger candidate than they are now; I hold them only as alternatives.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no known collaboration or personal tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang authors or the alternatives. My field, theoretical magnetism and DFT, is close to the electronic-structure side of B013, which is expertise and not a conflict. I request no recusal and know of no recusal request on B013.
